1. 
Injury in Fact as a Constitutional Requirement. Although by the time 
Lujan was decided it had become uncontroversial that the injury in fact 
requirement is rooted in Article Ill’s “case or controversy” requirement, this 
was not always the case. Note that in Sierra Club v. Morton, the Supreme 
Court seemed to treat the injury in fact requirement as a gloss on the judicial 
review provision of the APA. Two years earlier, in ADAPSO, it appeared to be 
a gloss on Article III. In 1973, the Supreme Court again treated injury in fact 
as an interpretation of the APA. See United States v. Students Challenging 
Regulatory Agency Procedures (SCRAP), 412 U.S. 669, 686, 689 n.l4. But in 
1974, a majority of the Supreme Court made clear that the injury in fact 
requirement was an interpretation of the case or controversy requirement of 
Article III and read ADAPSO to have established the point. Schlesinger v. 
Reservists Comm, to Stop the War, 418 U.S. 208, 218 (1974).
2. 
Particularized Injuries, Generalized Grievances, and Statutory 
Injuries. Sierra Club v. Morton and Lujan allow plaintiffs to assert widely 
shared injuries, but the courts insist that the plaintiffs identify with 
particularity their experience of that injury. The Court’s primary articulated 
reason for demanding a particularized injury to support standing is avoiding 
lawsuits that amount essentially to pohtical grievances, which could be 
addressed through pohtical processes. Thus, in United States v. Richardson, 
418 U.S. 166 (1974), the Court dismissed a taxpayer’s suit to challenge the 
nonpubhcation of the CIA’s budget under the “statement and account” clause 
of Article I, section 9 of the Constitution for lack of standing. The Court 
described the taxpayer’s alleged injury—disabling him from voting with 
knowledge of incumbent legislators’ decisions about intelhgence budgeting— 
as a mere “generalized grievance” that failed to distinguish him from any 
citizen who objected to the secrecy of the intelhgence budget. The Court dealt 
similarly that year with a chaUenge to the reserve officer status of certain 
members of Congress. The plaintiffs there aheged that holding such 
commissions contravened the “Incompatibihty Clause,” U.S. CONST., art. I, § 6, 
which precludes members of Congress from simultaneously holding any office 
in the executive branch. Schlesinger v. Reservists Comm, to Stop the War, 418 
U.S. 208 (1974).
